title: A Venus flytrap counts: two touches to shut, five to start digesting
body: Each lobe of the trap carries three tiny trigger hairs. One touch alone does nothing, which stops the plant wasting energy on a raindrop or a drifting leaf. If a second hair is touched within about **20 seconds**, or the same hair twice in quick succession, the lobes snap shut in roughly a tenth of a second. A struggling insect keeps brushing the hairs, and once the count reaches five the plant starts producing digestive enzymes. Digestion takes about ten days, after which the trap reopens and drops the empty husk.

slides.alt: Diagram of an open Venus flytrap with three trigger hairs on each lobe, above a counter: one touch does nothing, two touches within 20 seconds shut the trap in about 0.1 seconds, five touches start digestion.
slides.caption: The trap keeps a count of touches before it acts.

slides.question: How many days does a Venus flytrap take to digest a catch?
slides.explanation: Digestion takes about ten days. Then the trap reopens and releases the empty husk, ready for the next meal.

slides.heading: The count
items: Touch 1: nothing happens. It could be rain.
Touch 2 within 20 s: the lobes shut in about 0.1 s
Touch 5: digestive enzymes start to flow
About 10 days later the trap reopens

slides.question: Out of 10 creatures a Venus flytrap catches, how many are ants?
slides.explanation: About 33%, by a count of its prey, with 30% spiders, 10% beetles and 10% grasshoppers. Flying insects make up fewer than 5% of what the ‘flytrap’ actually eats.

slides.heading: Flies, mostly not
slides.text: Despite the name, flying insects make up under 5% of its catch. A study of its prey found about 33% ants, 30% spiders, 10% beetles and 10% grasshoppers. In the wild the plant grows only in a patch of the coastal Carolinas, within roughly 100 km of Wilmington, North Carolina.
